apis.name: CreateFileW
apis.summary: Creates or opens a file, device, pipe, or other I/O object and returns a handle.
apis.description: CreateFileW is the general entry point for obtaining a handle to a file-system object or device. The requested access, share mode, creation disposition, and flags determine what the handle can do and how the object is treated. Despite the name, the function opens existing objects as often as it creates new ones; OPEN_EXISTING is used when the file must already be present, and CREATE_ALWAYS replaces an existing file.
apis.prototype: HANDLE CreateFileW(LPCWSTR lpFileName, DWORD dwDesiredAccess, DWORD dwShareMode, LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES lpSecurityAttributes, DWORD dwCreationDisposition, DWORD dwFlagsAndAttributes, HANDLE hTemplateFile);

parameters.name: lpFileName
parameters.description: The name of the file or device to create or open. Forward and backslashes are both accepted. By default the name is limited to MAX_PATH characters; prepend \\?\ to extend the limit to 32,767 wide characters. Device paths such as \\.\C: address volumes rather than ordinary files.

parameters.name: dwDesiredAccess
parameters.description: The requested access, most commonly GENERIC_READ, GENERIC_WRITE, or both. A value of zero requests attribute-only access without reading or writing the object.

parameters.name: dwShareMode
parameters.description: The sharing mode for the object. Zero requests exclusive access; FILE_SHARE_READ, FILE_SHARE_WRITE, and FILE_SHARE_DELETE permit the corresponding concurrent access. A conflicting existing open causes ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION.

parameters.name: lpSecurityAttributes
parameters.description: An optional SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES structure. NULL gives the handle a default security descriptor and makes it non-inheritable. When opening an existing object, the security descriptor member is ignored but the inheritance flag still applies.

parameters.name: dwCreationDisposition
parameters.description: One of CREATE_NEW, CREATE_ALWAYS, OPEN_EXISTING, OPEN_ALWAYS, or TRUNCATE_EXISTING. The values cannot be combined. Use OPEN_EXISTING to open a file only if it exists, and CREATE_ALWAYS to create or replace it.

parameters.name: dwFlagsAndAttributes
parameters.description: File attributes and flags, such as FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED for asynchronous I/O, or FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS when opening a directory. FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL is valid only when no other attribute is set.

parameters.name: hTemplateFile
parameters.description: An optional handle to a template file opened with GENERIC_READ, whose attributes are applied to a newly created file. NULL is typical. The parameter is ignored when opening an existing object.

return.success: An open handle to the file, device, pipe, or other object. Close it with CloseHandle when finished.
return.failure: INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE, not NULL. Call GetLastError; ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND, ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND, and ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED are common.

apis.unicode_notes: CreateFileW is the Unicode variant. CreateFileA accepts an ANSI path, and the encoding-neutral CreateFile alias resolves to one of them at compile time based on UNICODE.
apis.remarks: Close the handle with CloseHandle; closing also affects sharing and can commit buffered data. To open a directory, use OPEN_EXISTING with FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS. A handle opened without FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED serializes I/O operations, even if an OVERLAPPED structure is supplied to a read or write call. Direct volume and device access has additional access and privilege requirements.
apis.maldev_notes: File creation and opening appear in virtually every Windows program. Analysts usually examine the path, access mask, disposition, and share mode together with what is subsequently read or written. Device paths and volume handles are less common than ordinary file paths and are worth noting when they appear in unexpected software.
apis.defensive_notes: File I/O telemetry, including ETW file providers and EDR file events where available, can record the path, requested access, and creation disposition. Unusual paths or access masks should be interpreted together with the process, user, and subsequent file activity.

apis.name: ReadFile
apis.summary: Reads data from a file or device into a buffer, starting at the current file position or at an explicit offset.
apis.description: ReadFile transfers bytes from a file, pipe, or device into a caller-supplied buffer. For a synchronous handle the file pointer advances by the number of bytes read; for an overlapped handle the offset comes from the OVERLAPPED structure. The function reports how many bytes were actually read, which can be smaller than the requested count.
apis.prototype: BOOL ReadFile(HANDLE hFile, LPVOID lpBuffer, DWORD nNumberOfBytesToRead, LPDWORD lpNumberOfBytesRead, LPOVERLAPPED lpOverlapped);

parameters.name: hFile
parameters.description: A handle to the file, pipe, or device to read. The handle must have been opened with read access, such as GENERIC_READ.

parameters.name: lpBuffer
parameters.description: A buffer that receives the data. It must be large enough for nNumberOfBytesToRead bytes.

parameters.name: nNumberOfBytesToRead
parameters.description: The maximum number of bytes to read. Zero is permitted and performs no read.

parameters.name: lpNumberOfBytesRead
parameters.description: Receives the number of bytes actually read. This parameter can be NULL only when lpOverlapped is not NULL, in which case the count is available from the OVERLAPPED structure after completion.

parameters.name: lpOverlapped
parameters.description: An optional OVERLAPPED structure that supplies a byte offset and, for asynchronous handles, an event used to signal completion. NULL performs a synchronous read at the current file position.

return.success: A nonzero value. Check lpNumberOfBytesRead, because the transfer may be shorter than requested; a synchronous read at end of file succeeds with zero bytes read.
return.failure: Zero. Call GetLastError. For an asynchronous operation, ERROR_IO_PENDING means the read is still in progress.

apis.remarks: A nonzero return with zero bytes read is the normal end-of-file indication for a synchronous read. Do not assume the requested byte count was transferred. For overlapped I/O, the buffer and OVERLAPPED structure must remain valid until the operation completes.
apis.maldev_notes: ReadFile is used by nearly all software that consumes file data. In analysis, the interesting details are usually which files are read, how much data is transferred, and whether the reads target unusual paths or raw devices rather than the call itself.
apis.defensive_notes: File-read telemetry is high volume on most systems. Baselining the files an application normally reads is usually more useful than flagging individual read operations; unusual volume or access to sensitive paths can then be reviewed in context.

apis.name: WriteFile
apis.summary: Writes data from a buffer to a file or device at the current position or at an explicit offset.
apis.description: WriteFile writes bytes from a caller buffer to a file, pipe, or device. For a synchronous handle the file pointer advances by the number of bytes written; for an overlapped handle the offset is taken from the OVERLAPPED structure. The function reports how many bytes were written.
apis.prototype: BOOL WriteFile(HANDLE hFile, LPCVOID lpBuffer, DWORD nNumberOfBytesToWrite, LPDWORD lpNumberOfBytesWritten, LPOVERLAPPED lpOverlapped);

parameters.name: hFile
parameters.description: A handle to the file, pipe, or device to write. The handle must have been opened with write access, such as GENERIC_WRITE.

parameters.name: lpBuffer
parameters.description: A buffer containing the data to write. The buffer must remain valid for the duration of the operation.

parameters.name: nNumberOfBytesToWrite
parameters.description: The number of bytes to write. Zero is permitted and performs no write.

parameters.name: lpNumberOfBytesWritten
parameters.description: Receives the number of bytes written. This parameter can be NULL only when lpOverlapped is not NULL, in which case the count is available from the OVERLAPPED structure after completion.

parameters.name: lpOverlapped
parameters.description: An optional OVERLAPPED structure that supplies a byte offset and, for asynchronous handles, an event used to signal completion. NULL writes at the current file position for a synchronous handle.

return.success: A nonzero value. Check lpNumberOfBytesWritten for the number of bytes actually written.
return.failure: Zero. Call GetLastError. For an asynchronous operation, ERROR_IO_PENDING means the write is still in progress.

apis.remarks: Closing a handle does not by itself guarantee that all buffered data has reached persistent storage; call FlushFileBuffers when durability matters. Do not close a handle while an overlapped write that uses it is still pending. For a synchronous handle, writes occur at the current file pointer, which can be changed with SetFilePointerEx.
apis.maldev_notes: WriteFile appears whenever software produces file output, including logs, documents, installers, and extracted resources. Analysts often examine the written path and content in context rather than treating file writes as a signal on their own.
apis.defensive_notes: File-write telemetry can identify created or modified files, and is most useful when correlated with the creating process, the path, and subsequent execution or network activity involving the same file.
apis.source_notes: Prototype, overlapped-I/O rules, and buffering caveat checked against Microsoft Learn (fileapi.h).

apis.name: SetFilePointerEx
apis.summary: Moves the file pointer of a file handle by a signed 64-bit offset from a specified origin.
apis.description: SetFilePointerEx positions the file pointer used by subsequent synchronous I/O on a file handle. The new position is computed from an origin (FILE_BEGIN, FILE_CURRENT, or FILE_END) plus a signed 64-bit offset. On success the resulting absolute position can be returned to the caller. The Ex form avoids the separate high-word handling required by the older SetFilePointer function.
apis.prototype: BOOL SetFilePointerEx(HANDLE hFile, LARGE_INTEGER liDistanceToMove, PLARGE_INTEGER lpNewFilePointer, DWORD dwMoveMethod);

parameters.name: hFile
parameters.description: A handle to a file opened for reading or writing. The handle must refer to a seekable object; pipes and communications devices are not seekable.

parameters.name: liDistanceToMove
parameters.description: The signed 64-bit offset to apply, in bytes. A negative value moves backward when the origin is FILE_CURRENT or FILE_END.

parameters.name: lpNewFilePointer
parameters.description: An optional pointer that receives the new file pointer, as an absolute offset from the beginning of the file. NULL is permitted when the new position is not needed.

parameters.name: dwMoveMethod
parameters.description: The starting point for the offset: FILE_BEGIN (start of file), FILE_CURRENT (current position), or FILE_END (end of file).

return.success: A nonzero value; the file pointer has been updated.
return.failure: Zero. Call GetLastError; an attempt to move before the beginning of the file fails.

apis.remarks: Seeking beyond the end of a file does not extend the file until a write occurs. Use GetFileSizeEx rather than seeking to the end to measure a file. The function is not meaningful for nonseeking devices such as pipes.
apis.maldev_notes: Random access is ordinary for databases, archives, parsers, and file formats with indexes. In analysis, seek patterns can help reconstruct how a program traverses a structured file, especially when reads are not sequential.
apis.defensive_notes: Seek operations may supplement file-read telemetry when reconstructing how a file was parsed. They are not a standalone indicator and are most useful when tied to the handle's file and the surrounding reads.
apis.source_notes: Prototype, 64-bit offset semantics, and origin constants checked against Microsoft Learn (fileapi.h).

apis.name: GetFileSizeEx
apis.summary: Retrieves the size of a file as a 64-bit value.
apis.description: GetFileSizeEx returns the logical size, in bytes, of the file associated with a handle. Unlike the older GetFileSize function, it reports the full 64-bit size in a single LARGE_INTEGER output. The handle must have been opened with read or write access, as documented.
apis.prototype: BOOL GetFileSizeEx(HANDLE hFile, PLARGE_INTEGER lpFileSize);

parameters.name: hFile
parameters.description: A handle to the file. The handle must have been created with GENERIC_READ or GENERIC_WRITE access, and must refer to a file rather than a nonseeking device.

parameters.name: lpFileSize
parameters.description: Receives the file size in bytes as a signed 64-bit value.

return.success: A nonzero value; lpFileSize contains the file size.
return.failure: Zero. Call GetLastError. The function fails for handles to nonseeking devices such as pipes.

apis.remarks: The size is a snapshot and can change while the handle remains open. It describes the logical file size, not the space consumed on disk or the amount of data that can be read from a device.
apis.maldev_notes: File sizes are collected by installers, packers, and analysis tools alike. A size by itself says little; it is useful mainly alongside content, path, and process context.
apis.defensive_notes: File size is a low-cost metadata field available in many telemetry sources and is most useful for correlation, such as a file whose size changes shortly before execution.
apis.source_notes: Prototype, access requirement, and nonseeking-device limitation checked against Microsoft Learn (fileapi.h).

apis.name: CloseHandle
apis.summary: Closes an open handle to a file, process, thread, or other kernel object.
apis.description: CloseHandle releases a handle obtained from a handle-creating API. Closing the last handle to an object can destroy it; for files, the close also affects sharing and can commit buffered state. Not every handle must or can be closed: pseudo-handles such as those returned by GetCurrentProcess and GetCurrentThread must not be passed to CloseHandle.
apis.prototype: BOOL CloseHandle(HANDLE hObject);

parameters.name: hObject
parameters.description: A handle to an open object. It must have been returned by a function that creates or opens a closable kernel object, and it must not be a pseudo-handle or a handle already closed.

return.success: A nonzero value; the handle has been closed.
return.failure: Zero. Call GetLastError. Under a debugger, an invalid or pseudo-handle raises an exception instead of returning normally.

apis.remarks: Closing a handle does not guarantee that buffered file data has reached disk; call FlushFileBuffers before closing when durability is required. Do not close a handle while an asynchronous I/O operation that uses it is still pending. Closing a handle twice is an error and can affect an unrelated object if the handle value has been reused.
apis.maldev_notes: Handle cleanup is ordinary resource management found in well-behaved and poorly behaved software alike. Analysts more often care about which handles a process opened and how long they stayed open than about the close itself.
apis.defensive_notes: Handle lifecycle can help explain when a file was released or an object was destroyed, particularly in timelines assembled from ETW or EDR events. It is rarely interesting in isolation.
apis.source_notes: Prototype, pseudo-handle caveat, and debugger exception behavior checked against Microsoft Learn (handleapi.h).

apis.name: ConnectNamedPipe
apis.summary: Enables a named pipe server process to wait for a client process to connect to an instance of a named pipe.
apis.description: Enables a named pipe server process to wait for a client process to connect to an instance of a named pipe. A client process connects by calling either the CreateFile or CallNamedPipe function.
apis.prototype: BOOL ConnectNamedPipe(HANDLE hNamedPipe, LPOVERLAPPED lpOverlapped);

parameters.name: hNamedPipe
parameters.description: A handle to the server end of a named pipe instance. This handle is returned by the CreateNamedPipe function.

parameters.name: lpOverlapped
parameters.description: A pointer to an OVERLAPPED structure. If hNamedPipe was opened with FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, the lpOverlapped parameter must not be NULL. It must point to a valid OVERLAPPED structure. If hNamedPipe was opened with FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED and lpOverlapped is NULL, the function can incorrectly report that the connect operation is complete. If hNamedPipe was created with FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED and lpOverlapped is not NULL, the OVERLAPPED structure should contain a handle to a manual-reset event object (which the server can create by using the CreateEvent function). If hNamedPipe was not opened with FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, the function does not return until a client is connected or an error occurs. Successful synchronous operations result in the function returning a nonzero value if a client connects after the function is called.

return.success: If the operation is synchronous, ConnectNamedPipe does not return until the operation has completed. If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero. If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call GetLastError.
return.failure: If the operation is asynchronous, ConnectNamedPipe returns immediately. If the operation is still pending, the return value is zero and GetLastError returns ERROR_IO_PENDING. (You can use the HasOverlappedIoCompleted macro to determine when the operation has finished.) If the function fails, the return value is zero and GetLastError returns a value other than ERROR_IO_PENDING or ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED. If a client connects before the function is called, the function returns zero and GetLastError returns ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED. This can happen if a client connects in the interval between the call to CreateNamedPipe and the call to ConnectNamedPipe. In this situation, there is a good connection between client and server, even though the function returns zero.

apis.remarks: A named pipe server process can use ConnectNamedPipe with a newly created pipe instance. It can also be used with an instance that was previously connected to another client process; in this case, the server process must first call the DisconnectNamedPipe function to disconnect the handle from the previous client before the handle can be reconnected to a new client. Otherwise, ConnectNamedPipe returns zero, and GetLastError returns ERROR_NO_DATA if the previous client has closed its handle or ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED if it has not closed its handle. The behavior of ConnectNamedPipe depends on two conditions: whether the pipe handle's wait mode is set to blocking or nonblocking and whether the function is set to execute synchronously or in overlapped mode. A server initially specifies a pipe handle's wait mode in the CreateNamedPipe function, and it can be changed by using the SetNamedPipeHandleState function. The server process can use any of the wait functions or SleepEx— to determine when the state of the event object is signaled, and it can then use the HasOverlappedIoCompleted macro to determine when the ConnectNamedPipe operation completes. If the specified pipe handle is in nonblocking mode, ConnectNamedPipe always returns immediately. apis.summary: Copies an existing file to a new file.
apis.description: Copies an existing file to a new file. The CopyFileEx function provides two additional capabilities. CopyFileEx can call a specified callback function each time a portion of the copy operation is completed, and CopyFileEx can be canceled during the copy operation. To perform this operation as a transacted operation, use the CopyFileTransacted function.
apis.prototype: BOOL CopyFileA(LPCSTR lpExistingFileName, LPCSTR lpNewFileName, BOOL bFailIfExists);

parameters.name: lpExistingFileName
parameters.description: The name of an existing file. By default, the name is limited to MAX_PATH characters. To extend this limit to 32,767 wide characters, prepend "\\?\" to the path. If lpExistingFileName does not exist, CopyFile fails, and GetLastError returns ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND.

parameters.name: lpNewFileName
parameters.description: The name of the new file. By default, the name is limited to MAX_PATH characters. To extend this limit to 32,767 wide characters, prepend "\\?\" to the path. See the "Maximum Path Length Limitation" section of Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces for details.

parameters.name: bFailIfExists
parameters.description: If this parameter is TRUE and the new file specified by lpNewFileName already exists, the function fails. If this parameter is FALSE and the new file already exists, the function overwrites the existing file and succeeds.

return.success: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
return.failure: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call GetLastError.

Value Meaning COPY_FILE_ALLOW_DECRYPTED_DESTINATION 0x00000008 An attempt to copy an encrypted file will succeed even if the destination copy cannot be encrypted. apis.name: GetFileTime
apis.summary: Retrieves the date and time that a file or directory was created, last accessed, and last modified.
apis.description: Retrieves the date and time that a file or directory was created, last accessed, and last modified.
apis.prototype: BOOL GetFileTime(HANDLE hFile, LPFILETIME lpCreationTime, LPFILETIME lpLastAccessTime, LPFILETIME lpLastWriteTime);

parameters.name: hFile
parameters.description: A handle to the file or directory for which dates and times are to be retrieved. The handle must have been created using the CreateFile function with the GENERIC_READ access right. For more information, see File Security and Access Rights.

parameters.name: lpCreationTime
parameters.description: A pointer to a FILETIME structure to receive the date and time the file or directory was created. This parameter can be NULL if the application does not require this information.

parameters.name: lpLastAccessTime
parameters.description: A pointer to a FILETIME structure to receive the date and time the file or directory was last accessed. The last access time includes the last time the file or directory was written to, read from, or, in the case of executable files, run. This parameter can be NULL if the application does not require this information.

parameters.name: lpLastWriteTime
parameters.description: A pointer to a FILETIME structure to receive the date and time the file or directory was last written to, truncated, or overwritten (for example, with WriteFile or SetEndOfFile). This date and time is not updated when file attributes or security descriptors are changed. This parameter can be NULL if the application does not require this information.

return.success: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
return.failure: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call GetLastError.

apis.remarks: Not all file systems can record creation and last access times and not all file systems record them in the same manner. For example, on FAT, create time has a resolution of 10 milliseconds, write time has a resolution of 2 seconds, and access time has a resolution of 1 day (really, the access date). Therefore, the GetFileTime function may not return the same file time information set using the SetFileTime function. NTFS delays updates to the last access time for a file by up to one hour after the last access. NTFS also permits last access time updates to be disabled. Last access time is not updated on NTFS volumes by default. Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: Last access time is updated on NTFS volumes by default. For more information, see File Times. If you rename or delete a file, then restore it shortly thereafter, Windows searches the cache for file information to restore. Cached information includes its short/long name pair and creation time. #### Examples For an example, see Retrieving the Last-Write Time.

parameters.description: The null-terminated prefix string. The function uses up to the first three characters of this string as the prefix of the file name. This string must consist of characters in the OEM-defined character set.

parameters.description: An unsigned integer to be used in creating the temporary file name. For more information, see Remarks. If *uUnique* is zero, the function attempts to form a unique file name using the current system time. If the file already exists, the number is increased by one and the functions tests if this file already exists. This continues until a unique filename is found; the function creates a file by that name and closes it. Note that the function does not attempt to verify the uniqueness of the file name when *uUnique* is nonzero.

parameters.name: lpTempFileName
parameters.description: A pointer to the buffer that receives the temporary file name. This buffer should be MAX_PATH characters to accommodate the path plus the terminating null character.

apis.summary: Searches for a specified file in a specified path.
apis.description: Searches for a specified file in a specified path.

parameters.name: lpPath
parameters.description: The path to be searched for the file. If this parameter is NULL, the function searches for a matching file using a registry-dependent system search path. For more information, see the Remarks section.

parameters.name: lpFileName
parameters.description: The name of the file for which to search. By default, the name is limited to MAX_PATH characters. To extend this limit to 32,767 wide characters, prepend "\\?\" to the path. For more information, see Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces. > > Starting with Windows 10, Version 1607, you can opt-in to remove the MAX_PATH limitation without prepending "\\?\". See the "Maximum Path Length Limitation" section of Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces for details.

parameters.name: lpExtension
parameters.description: The extension to be added to the file name when searching for the file. The first character of the file name extension must be a period (.). The extension is added only if the specified file name does not end with an extension. If a file name extension is not required or if the file name contains an extension, this parameter can be NULL.

parameters.name: nBufferLength
parameters.description: The size of the buffer that receives the valid path and file name (including the terminating null character), in TCHARs.

parameters.name: lpBuffer
parameters.description: A pointer to the buffer to receive the path and file name of the file found. The string is a null-terminated string.

parameters.name: lpFilePart
parameters.description: A pointer to the variable to receive the address (within lpBuffer) of the last component of the valid path and file name, which is the address of the character immediately following the final backslash (\) in the path.

return.success: If the function succeeds, the value returned is the length, in TCHARs, of the string that is copied to the buffer, not including the terminating null character. If the return value is greater than nBufferLength, the value returned is the size of the buffer that is required to hold the path, including the terminating null character.
return.failure: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call GetLastError.

apis.remarks: If the lpPath parameter is NULL, SearchPath searches for a matching file based on the current value of the following registry value: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\SafeProcessSearchMode When the value of this REG_DWORD registry value is set to 1, SearchPath first searches the folders that are specified in the system path, and then searches the current working folder. When the value of this registry value is set to 0, the computer first searches the current working folder, and then searches the folders that are specified in the system path. The system default value for this registry key is 0. The search mode used by the SearchPath function can also be set per-process by calling the SetSearchPathMode function. The SearchPath function is not recommended as a method of locating a .dll file if the intended use of the output is in a call to the LoadLibrary function. This can result in locating the wrong .dll file because the search order of the SearchPath function differs from the search order used by the LoadLibrary function. If you need to locate and load a .dll file, use the LoadLibrary function. In Windows 8 and Windows Server 2012, this function is supported by the following technologies. apis.name: SetFileTime
apis.summary: Sets the date and time that the specified file or directory was created, last accessed, or last modified.
apis.description: Sets the date and time that the specified file or directory was created, last accessed, or last modified.
apis.prototype: BOOL SetFileTime(HANDLE hFile, CONST FILETIME* lpCreationTime, CONST FILETIME* lpLastAccessTime, CONST FILETIME* lpLastWriteTime);

parameters.name: hFile
parameters.description: A handle to the file or directory. The handle must have been created using the CreateFile function with the FILE_WRITE_ATTRIBUTES access right. For more information, see File Security and Access Rights.

parameters.name: lpCreationTime
parameters.description: A pointer to a FILETIME structure that contains the new creation date and time for the file or directory. If the application does not need to change this information, set this parameter either to NULL or to a pointer to a FILETIME structure that has both the dwLowDateTime and dwHighDateTime members set to 0.

parameters.name: lpLastAccessTime
parameters.description: A pointer to a FILETIME structure that contains the new last access date and time for the file or directory. The last access time includes the last time the file or directory was written to, read from, or (in the case of executable files) run. If the application does not need to change this information, set this parameter either to NULL or to a pointer to a FILETIME structure that has both the dwLowDateTime and dwHighDateTime members set to 0. To prevent file operations using the given handle from modifying the last access time, call SetFileTime immediately after opening the file handle and pass a FILETIME structure that has both the dwLowDateTime and dwHighDateTime members set to 0xFFFFFFFF.

parameters.name: lpLastWriteTime
parameters.description: A pointer to a FILETIME structure that contains the new last modified date and time for the file or directory. If the application does not need to change this information, set this parameter either to NULL or to a pointer to a FILETIME structure that has both the dwLowDateTime and dwHighDateTime members set to 0. To prevent file operations using the given handle from modifying the last write time, call SetFileTime immediately after opening the file handle and pass a FILETIME structure that has both the dwLowDateTime and dwHighDateTime members set to 0xFFFFFFFF.

return.success: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
return.failure: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call GetLastError.

apis.remarks: Not all file systems can record creation and last access times and not all file systems record them in the same manner. For example, on FAT, create time has a resolution of 10 milliseconds, write time has a resolution of 2 seconds, and access time has a resolution of 1 day (really, the access date). Therefore, the GetFileTime function may not return the same file time information set using SetFileTime. NTFS delays updates to the last access time for a file by up to one hour after the last access. ### Examples For an example, see Changing a File Time to the Current Time.
